Oct 13, 2026 56 9 Share Hi folks, quick aside: I’m working on something for non-developers who don’t quite know what to use personal agents for. Maybe you chat with it but you’re not quite seeing why everyone’s raving about them. If that’s you, please reply to this email. I’m looking for ~20 people to test a new thing. I’ll invite you to a slack channel. Ok so X is arguing whether software is dead…again. These takes are like assholes, everyone’s got one. Including me. Software isn’t dead. More code is being written than ever before (probably). Something may be dead, but we just don’t quite what it is. I use far fewer SaaS tools than I ever have before - I actually got my personal agent (grok bot btw) to go through our business subscriptions and saved $6k/year - got rid of webflow, resend, cal, zoom and a bunch more. If I do want to use any tools, I now think of whether my bots can use it. I never have to look at the interface, it’s all done by software talking to software - aka ‘headless’. And I’m making sites for all sorts of things. I spun up a site to review all my subscriptions so I could easily go through them and mark which to keep or kill. Then I just throw away the site after I use it. (or more accurately, it just sits somewhere untouched forever). The biggest problem I see is that most people don’t see themselves as ‘builders’. They don’t think to build a site for tasks (todos, email triage, recipes, kids calendars, etc). But that’s my default. I hate reading words, ironically. Give me something visual any day. I think agents will be the form factor that gets everyday people to make software, as long as it doesn’t feel like it. The problem right now is those agents are proactive (sometimes) that give you work to do (aren’t you working for me!?) and they don’t hand you software unless you ask for it. If you were given a site with your todos, I’d bet you’d want to customise the colours or layout or something. When we had MySpace pages we customised them with music, themes, layouts. Some people went further and learnt HTML & CSS to customise further. Software ‘you’ create should just feel like customising something that’s already yours. Other related things I’ve been thinking about: slop is a slur, as is vibe coding . Developers love to shit on us for our agents writing slop code. But if it works, is secure and performant, why does it really matter? It matters more if you’re providing critical infra for customers paying you money, sure. But for your own tools and sites, slop works. I also believe it’s an agents job to deal with slop, my code is bad? cool - go fix it then. slop → slope . You know how developers started? Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,313 211 136 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. Dots and Muse The number one app in the App Store right now is Meta’s Muse, a personal agent that promises to do work for you. OpenAI has now released a competitor tool, called dots. They aren’t alone: SpaceX’s Grok Bot, Instinct, and Gemini Spark all do similar things, more or less. All of these agents draw inspiration from a phenomenon you might remember from earlier this year, OpenClaw. content: The Overhang - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Overhang Using your deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste, and agency Ethan Mollick Sep 18, 2026 936 109 101 Share We are still on an exponential curve of AI development. I try to put out a Substack post every couple weeks or so, yet, as the pace speeds up, that sometimes feels too slow. In the weeks since my last post, we had the apparent cracking of one of the most famous problems in math by an AI (accompanied by controversy) and widespread discussions about the risks posed by AI and what to do about it (also accompanied by controversy). I think these concerns, along with a mounting set of other worries, come down to the same problem I have with my posts: how slowly our very human systems and processes work to keep up with the pace of AI development. I don't think the people worried about this are wrong, but I also think a sole focus on future AIs, as important as that is, ignores the fact that AI, right now, is already incredibly capable. In fact, the new GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 are already enough for transformative impact in large sections of the economy and they can reliably do weeks worth of human work when properly guided and harnessed. A few fun examples of that: I had GPT-6 Astra turn a 1977 text adventure game called Zork into a full 3D action-adventure game you can play . Zork has no graphics and each location is a paragraph of prose, so the AI had to decide what the white house looks like, what a grue looks like (the original only tells you that you are likely to be eaten by one in the dark), and how to turn “fight the troll” into an action sequence. I also had Fable 5.1 try to reconstruct Italian author Umberto Eco’s library in 3D . Eco kept tens of thousands of books in his Milan apartment and the AI could not find a floor plan, so it instead decided to work from a dozen videos, the foundation's photographs of each bookcase, and two library catalogues. It read spines frame by frame, inferred the rooms, and placed the 5,000 or so books it could identify among 27,000 shelf slots. It marked every book certain, guess, or unknown, and drew the bookcases the cameras never reached in fog. This task, like the Zork game and a lot of real-world work I have had the AI do recently, would have taken weeks of human work involving researchers, coders, and designers. But here we are. content: Latest open artifacts (#25): DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, American-made models, and new regulatory controls in the US & China Subscribe Sign in Latest open artifacts (#25): DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, American-made models, and new regulatory controls in the US & China A maturing open model ecosystem steps towards regulatory uncertainty. Florian Brand and Nathan Lambert Oct 20, 2026 ∙ Paid 19 5 2 Share The geopolitics of open-weight AI are accelerating again this fall, as we would expect with the risks of all AI systems (open and closed) rising rapidly. We’ve seen many news items in the last week showing both the U.S. and Chinese governments positioning themselves for some controls on open models. MOFCOM, the Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China, released a policy proposal (it’s not yet a law) that would require frontier AI models and some other technologies to get pre-approval from the government before they can be shared internationally. We found the reaction to this to be overblown – as the document states that open-source technologies will be set up for automatic approvals – but many in geopolitical circles say this is a big deal because it proposes a regulatory framework that could be used in the future to regulate China’s AI industry. Others we trust on this issue say this proposal could be more about preventing issues like the sale of Chinese startup Manus to Western companies, rather than being about frontier AI models. Either way, the wheels of control are moving around AI, and open-weight models are not free from any influence. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released an order on DeepSeek , which restricts DeepSeek itself, as a company, and DeepSeek’s models, as a technology platform, from being a vendor in federal civilian procurement. It is not clear how this will relate to finetuned models or models trained on the outputs of DeepSeek (e.g., Nvidia’s Nemotron models have long relied heavily on DeepSeek models in their training recipes – will they be banned?), but this is an expected action and reinforces the need for a domestic open model ecosystem. Other model makers in China, such as Zhipu AI, makers of GLM, are already on the Entity List under Commerce/BIS, which restricts their access to American technology. DeepSeek followed the above news up by releasing their internal inference stack publicly, DeepInfer , which is likely far more efficient than existing open-source tools like vLLM/SGLang for their models. Estimates point to DeepSeek making up to 90% gross margin when selling tokens on this inference stack. It is well-known that the top AI labs have much more inference-efficient tools internally, and this is the first time we’ve seen a leading lab share them. Inference companies will be quick to adopt these tools, which will drive prices for DeepSeek’s models down across the ecosystem (or margins up). content: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed Subscribe Sign in Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed US open weights are back! Nathan Lambert Oct 17, 2026 78 13 11 Share Article voiceover 0:00 -11:43 Audio playback is not supported on your browser. Please upgrade. This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier. Meta took the lead of this charge with Muse Spark Open , which is now the strongest American-made open model by quite some margin, but the addition of Reflection’s first model Beam is also relevant. Without these two models, there would be 20+ open-weight models built and released by Chinese companies better than the best Western models. At the time of writing this, Mistral has also announced a strong model, Mistral Large 4 , with an index score of 38 (see below), but its weights are not yet released. There are rumors of a few more strong American open-weight models coming from other organizations too! In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant. This paints the picture of the cut-throat, competitive nature of the frontier model business. Reflection and Mistral announced their model scores and Meta dropped the weights of a smarter model before these other two labs could get their own weights out. All of these models are competing with Chinese models released months ago, where the industry is collectively asking — where have Kimi and Zhipu AI been since the releases of GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 on Aug. 18th and Jul. 16th, respectively? That is a very nuanced question, which I’ll dig into another time. Today’s piece is focused on Meta’s turnaround, what Muse Spark Open means for the ecosystem, and the balance of power across Western frontier labs. Share Why Muse Spark Open should take off — and why it may not One thing we see again and again at Interconnects through our open model analysis is that Western open-weight models get astonishingly more adoption than Chinese models with the same performance-to-size footprint (even though the Chinese models usually come out first)! Muse Spark Open is landing into this environment, at the same time as when open-ended LLM agents are finally real (~ GLM 5.2 capabilities and on ). Riding off a rapid increase in performance of Chinese models, the open ecosystem has been living through an acceleration in demand. The inference providers are rapidly scaling, the open post-training economy is forming, and countless enterprises are looking to own their intelligence. Muse Spark Open’s performance falls somewhere above GLM 5.2, near DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and behind GLM 5.3 or Kimi K3. It should be squarely “good enough” to slot right into this. title: <![CDATA[I expect rapid progress but not towards general superintelligence]]>
summary: I’ve often been surprised when I hear from top researchers in industry that they think AI will be better than them at their job in a few years, and I didn’t really know why I doubted it. The explanation I arrived at is that researchers are seeing this massive acceleration in the infra and engineerin...
content: I expect rapid progress but not towards general superintelligence Subscribe Sign in I expect rapid progress but not towards general superintelligence Musings on RSI after a week in SF. Nathan Lambert Oct 09, 2026 ∙ Paid 96 4 9 Share Upgrade to paid to play voiceover I’ve often been surprised when I hear from top researchers in industry that they think AI will be better than them at their job in a few years, and I didn’t really know why I doubted it. The explanation I arrived at is that researchers are seeing this massive acceleration in the infra and engineering capabilities of the models. I fully agree that the models will be superhuman distributed GPU engineers in a few years. This will make experimentation and tinkering with the formulation of the models far easier, but it will not make our models dramatically different in nature. In some ways, Ilya was early in his declaration of AI being in the era of research . Research is much easier today now that we have coding agents. This ease is through a different form of work that is flexible and engaging, which signals the start of an era where good ideas can be much more valuable than good execution in software. Subscribe We’re very early on this path. It’s also not the first transition the field has seen across the balance in if AI is more “research” or “engineering.” Before deep learning took off, AI was also far more of a research endeavor. Today, the best researchers are well-known to be judged by their ability to implement and scale their ideas in complex infrastructure. We’re about to go through a massive acceleration over a few years where the bottleneck is less and less engineering again. Some call this RSI, but a more grounded form is simply “parallelized, AI-assisted language modeling.” You don’t need to buy into takeoff scenarios to see just how much infrastructure improvements are coming, and how this’ll change the nature of working in AI. The goal of this piece is to give an overview on why this engineering acceleration will happen, and touch on what it won’t quite fix. This’ll be a massive boon for diffusion of the technology into the economy, even if we don’t get economically valuable superhuman traits outside of math and coding. A lot of this near-term progress comes from scaling the inference-time compute we have with current tools, rather than dramatic step-changes in how good the models are at research. Share Many pieces of the AI training and inference stack are very verifiable. Training metrics like tokens per second per GPU, which is just training speed. Inference metrics look like tokens per prompt, FLOPs per token, or really just cost per answer. Both of these are very optimizable, especially as there are established sub-problems and architecture trade-offs which can improve them. I expect AI agents to help optimize this process end-to-end in a few years, where our inference capabilities get very close to the underlying maximum compute possible on our accelerators like GPUs
